items.name: THE FLOPPY DISK
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 3.5-inch floppy disk
items.epitaph: Once found on every desk; now preserved inside the Save icon.
items.why: Smaller, faster, and vastly larger storage made its tiny capacity and fragile magnetic media impractical.
items.afterlife: Specialist manufacturers, old machinery, collectors, and one remarkably durable icon keep it alive.
items.note: 2011 marks the end of Sony's 3.5-inch floppy production, not the disappearance of every floppy disk.

items.name: CONCORDE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of Concorde in flight
items.epitaph: The future crossed the Atlantic faster than sound, then returned to subsonic speed.
items.why: High operating costs, limited routes, falling demand, and the aftermath of the 2000 crash ended commercial service.
items.afterlife: All surviving aircraft are preserved; none remains airworthy for passenger service.
items.note: The lifespan runs from first flight to final commercial service.

items.name: GOOGLE READER
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of an RSS feed reader
items.epitaph: It organized the open web before algorithms decided what we should read.
items.why: Google retired the service as usage declined while the company narrowed its product focus.
items.afterlife: RSS survived in independent readers, podcasts, and a smaller but stubbornly open ecosystem.
items.note: Google Reader closed on 1 July 2013.

items.name: THE iPOD
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a click-wheel music player
items.epitaph: A thousand songs left the pocket when the pocket became a phone.
items.why: Music playback became one function of the iPhone and other connected devices instead of a separate product.
items.afterlife: Used iPods, repair communities, and the click wheel preserve a distraction-free way to listen.
items.note: Apple ended the product line after selling remaining iPod touch stock.

items.name: ADOBE FLASH PLAYER
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a browser plug-in being removed
items.epitaph: For a while, the web moved, played, and wasted lunch breaks inside one browser plug-in.
items.why: Open web standards matured while security, performance, and mobile compatibility made the plug-in model untenable.
items.afterlife: Preservation projects and emulators keep thousands of Flash games and animations accessible.
items.note: Adobe ended support on 31 December 2020.

items.name: THE SPACE SHUTTLE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a Space Shuttle orbiter over Earth
items.epitaph: It made orbit look almost routine. It never truly was.
items.why: NASA completed the program after 30 years, shifting resources toward new spacecraft and exploration goals.
items.afterlife: The surviving orbiters are museum exhibits, while their engineering legacy continues across human spaceflight.
items.note: The final mission, STS-135, ended on 21 July 2011.

items.name: PAN AM
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 1970s jumbo jet at an airport
items.epitaph: Its blue globe once meant that the wider world was finally within reach.
items.why: Deregulation, rising costs, debt, and the loss of key assets left the pioneering airline unable to continue.
items.afterlife: Its routes, terminals, branding, and jet-age mythology remain embedded in commercial aviation history.
items.note: Pan American World Airways ceased operations in December 1991.

items.name: THE PASSENGER PIGEON
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history illustration of a passenger pigeon
items.epitaph: Billions filled the sky. Within a human lifetime, not one remained.
items.why: Industrial-scale hunting and destruction of its forest habitat drove a once-abundant species to extinction.
items.afterlife: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, is preserved at the Smithsonian.
items.source_name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
items.note: Martha died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914.

items.name: THE GREAT AUK
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history illustration of a great auk
items.epitaph: A flightless bird of the North Atlantic, collected until there was nothing left to collect.
items.why: Centuries of hunting for food, feathers, oil, and specimens eliminated the species from its nesting islands.
items.afterlife: Skins, skeletons, eggs, and museum records are all that remain.
items.note: The last widely accepted breeding pair was killed in Iceland in 1844.

items.name: BLOCKBUSTER VIDEO STORES
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 1990s video-rental store
items.epitaph: Friday-night choice once required fluorescent light, plastic cases, and a little negotiation.
items.why: Streaming and mail-order rentals replaced the cost and inconvenience of maintaining thousands of physical stores.
items.afterlife: One independently owned Blockbuster store still trades in Bend, Oregon.
items.note: The brand is not literally extinct; the Bend store remains open.

items.name: THE THYLACINE
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history illustration of a thylacine
items.epitaph: The last one died in captivity after the wild had already fallen silent.
items.why: Direct human persecution was the main cause, compounded by habitat change, introduced dogs, and other pressures.
items.afterlife: Film, photographs, museum specimens, and Tasmania's identity preserve the animal's unmistakable stripes.
items.note: The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo in 1936; later reported sightings remain unconfirmed.

items.name: THE OPPORTUNITY ROVER
items.image_alt: Monochrome technical illustration of NASA's Opportunity rover on Mars
items.epitaph: Built for ninety Martian days, it kept exploring until Mars finally went silent.
items.why: A planet-wide dust storm blocked sunlight, and NASA ended recovery attempts after months without contact.
items.afterlife: Its images, discoveries, scientific record, and tracks on Mars preserve nearly fifteen years of exploration.
items.note: Launched in 2003, Opportunity last communicated in June 2018; NASA declared the mission complete in February 2019.

items.name: THE SEARS BIG BOOK
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of an enormous open Sears mail-order catalogue
items.epitaph: Before online shopping, almost everything imaginable arrived inside one enormous book.
items.why: Shopping shifted toward stores and electronic commerce while the enormous general catalogue grew costly to produce.
items.afterlife: Digitised editions, surviving catalogues, mail-order houses, and museums preserve its inventory of American life.
items.note: Sears issued its first catalogue in 1888 and ceased production of the Big Book on 25 January 1993; specialised catalogues had different timelines.

items.name: VINE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 2010s smartphone recording a short looping video
items.epitaph: Six seconds was enough time to invent an entire language of comedy.
items.why: Twitter discontinued Vine as creators and audiences shifted to rival video platforms with broader formats and monetisation.
items.afterlife: Catchphrases, compilations, archived clips, and the short-loop format remain embedded in internet culture.
items.note: The original Vine social network became Vine Camera on 17 January 2017; later services using the name are separate revivals.

items.name: SATURN V
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a Saturn V rocket standing on its mobile launcher
items.epitaph: It carried people to the Moon, then launched America's first space station—and never flew again.
items.why: After Apollo and Skylab, cancelled lunar missions and changing priorities left no mission for another Saturn V.
items.afterlife: Preserved flight-certified stages, museum displays, records, and successor rockets carry its engineering legacy.
items.note: The first Saturn V launched in 1967; the thirteenth and final flight launched Skylab on 14 May 1973. Smithsonian records confirm preserved flight-certified stages.

items.name: THE WESTERN UNION TELEGRAM
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a telegraph printer, telegram, envelope, and Morse key
items.epitaph: Every word cost money, so important news learned to travel without small talk.
items.why: Telephone, fax, email, and instant messaging made hand-delivered telegrams slow and uneconomical.
items.afterlife: Forms, terse writing conventions, archives, and other providers preserve the medium and its ceremonial uses.
items.note: Western Union discontinued its telegram service on 27 January 2006. Other companies continued sending telegrams, so the subject remains company-specific.

items.name: THE ARECIBO TELESCOPE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of the intact Arecibo radio telescope and its three support towers
items.epitaph: For fifty-seven years it listened to the universe—until its own cables fell silent.
items.why: Progressive cable failures brought the suspended instrument platform down through the giant reflector dish.
items.afterlife: Its discoveries, archived data, surviving site facilities, and a new education centre preserve its legacy.
items.note: The 305-metre telescope opened in 1963 and collapsed on 1 December 2020. The wider observatory site survived; NSF later established Arecibo C3 there.

items.name: KODACHROME
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of 35 mm film, mounted slides, and a vintage slide projector
items.epitaph: The colours survived longer than the chemistry needed to make them.
items.why: Demand collapsed as photography moved to digital, while Kodachrome required a specialised development process.
items.afterlife: Decades of slides, scans, archives, and famous photographs preserve its distinctive colour palette.
items.note: Kodak ended production in 2009; the final commercial K-14 processing service ended in 2010.

items.name: THE PINTA ISLAND TORTOISE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a saddle-backed Pinta Island giant tortoise in volcanic habitat
items.epitaph: An entire lineage ended with one old tortoise called Lonesome George.
items.why: Centuries of hunting and introduced goats devastated the isolated Pinta population and its habitat.
items.afterlife: George remains a conservation symbol, while related hybrids may help restore parts of the lost lineage.
items.note: Lonesome George, the last known pure Pinta Island tortoise, died on 24 June 2012. Related hybrids retain some Pinta ancestry, so the subject remains the extinct pure lineage.

items.name: THE SWISS TELEPHONE BOOK
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of an open telephone directory and a rotary telephone
items.epitaph: For 142 years, finding someone began by turning thin pages.
items.why: Online directories, mobile phones, and fewer publicly listed private numbers made the printed book obsolete.
items.afterlife: Libraries, archives, and digitised directories preserve a detailed map of Swiss households and businesses.
items.note: The first Swiss directory appeared in Zurich in 1880; the final printed regional editions were issued in 2022.

items.name: NETFLIX DVD-BY-MAIL
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a postal DVD sleeve, disc, and residential mailbox
items.epitaph: Five billion red envelopes taught the mailbox how to compete with the video store.
items.why: Streaming replaced physical delivery, leaving the original subscription service as a shrinking side business.
items.afterlife: Discs, envelopes, queues, and memories remain after the streaming service outlived its postal ancestor.
items.note: The DVD-by-mail service began in 1998 and mailed its final discs on 29 September 2023. Netflix streaming continued.

items.name: GOOGLE STADIA
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a cloud-gaming controller, television, and remote servers
items.epitaph: The console lived in the cloud, but the cloud could still pull the plug.
items.why: The streaming platform failed to gain enough traction, so Google shut its stores and game servers.
items.afterlife: Refunds softened the ending, Bluetooth mode rescued controllers, and cloud gaming continued elsewhere.
items.note: Google announced the shutdown in September 2022 and kept Stadia servers online until 18 January 2023.

items.name: BLACKBERRY LEGACY DEVICES
items.epitaph: For a while, being important meant typing with both thumbs.
items.why: Touchscreen smartphones and app ecosystems displaced BlackBerry's keyboard-led platform before its legacy services ended.
items.afterlife: Preserved devices, the physical keyboard, collectors, and BlackBerry's security business keep the name familiar.
items.note: 1999 marks the first BlackBerry pager. 4 January 2022 marks legacy OS service retirement, not the end of Android devices or the company.
items.image_alt: Monochrome engraving of a BlackBerry Bold 9000 handset

items.name: ORIGINAL VW BEETLE
items.epitaph: Its shape survived fashion, borders, and generations—until the last one left Puebla.
items.why: Volkswagen ended Type 1 production after demand narrowed and newer cars replaced its ageing postwar design.
items.afterlife: Surviving Beetles are restored, collected, and driven; the final car is preserved in Volkswagen's museum.
items.note: Dates refer to postwar series production of the original Type 1; the last was produced in Puebla in 2003. The New Beetle and later Beetle are separate models.
items.image_alt: Monochrome engraving of an original Volkswagen Type 1 Beetle

items.name: SR-71 BLACKBIRD
items.epitaph: It crossed continents at Mach 3. Its final destination was the museum.
items.why: High operating costs and shrinking defence budgets ended its frontline role; NASA research flying continued until 1999.
items.afterlife: Preserved aircraft and flight records keep its extraordinary speed and engineering on display.
items.note: 1964 is first flight; 1999 is the final NASA flight. USAF initially retired it in 1990, briefly reactivated it, and retired it again in 1998.
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of an SR-71A Blackbird in flight

items.name: THE IKEA CATALOGUE
items.epitaph: For seventy years, the future of the living room arrived through the letterbox.
items.why: Customer behaviour moved online, reducing the purpose and readership of a huge annual printed catalogue.
items.afterlife: IKEA Museum has digitised the historical catalogues, turning decades of domestic design into an online archive.
items.note: Dates identify catalogue editions. The final 2021 edition was released in 2020; discontinuation was announced in December 2020.
items.image_alt: Interpretive monochrome illustration of an open furniture catalogue

items.name: THE GOLDEN TOAD
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a Golden Toad in Monteverde cloud forest
items.epitaph: A jewel-bright toad vanished from one small cloud forest in a single generation.
items.why: Its tiny range left it exposed; extreme dry weather and chytrid disease are leading explanations for the collapse.
items.afterlife: Museum specimens and its role as an emblem of the amphibian extinction crisis preserve its warning.
items.note: Discovered in 1964 and last seen in 1989; the asterisk marks the last sighting rather than an exact extinction date.

items.name: TUPOLEV TU-144 PASSENGER SERVICE
items.image_alt: Monochrome technical engraving of a Tu-144S airliner on final approach
items.epitaph: It promised a second supersonic future—and carried passengers for only seven months.
items.why: Operational difficulties and high costs ended passenger service after a fatal test-flight crash.
items.afterlife: Preserved aircraft and NASA’s later flying laboratory kept its remarkable engineering story airborne.
items.note: Passenger flights began in November 1977 and ended in 1978; cargo, test, and research flights continued later.

items.name: BBC CEEFAX
items.image_alt: Monochrome engraving of a period CRT television displaying a blocky teletext information page
items.epitaph: Before the web, news arrived one numbered page at a time.
items.why: The UK’s digital television switchover ended the analogue signal that carried the original teletext service.
items.afterlife: Archives, recreations, and its blocky visual language preserve a pre-web way of browsing information.
items.note: Ceefax launched on 23 September 1974 and ended with the final UK analogue television switchover on 23 October 2012.

items.name: CASSINI
items.epitaph: It became part of the world it had spent thirteen years revealing.
items.why: With fuel running low, Cassini was sent into Saturn to protect potentially habitable moons from contamination.
items.afterlife: Its images and scientific data keep revealing Saturn, its rings, and its moons long after the final signal.
items.note: Dates run from launch in 1997 to intentional atmospheric entry on 15 September 2017. This entry is the orbiter, not the Huygens lander.
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of the Cassini orbiter approaching Saturn

items.name: THE ORIGINAL PENN STATION
items.epitaph: New York tore down a gateway grand enough to make arrival feel like an event.
items.why: Declining rail traffic and a redevelopment deal traded its above-ground halls for Madison Square Garden.
items.afterlife: Surviving fragments, photographs, and the preservation movement born from its loss keep the station present.
items.source_name: Museum of the City of New York
items.note: 1963 marks the start of demolition; the above-ground building was removed by 1966 while the underground station continued.
items.image_alt: Monochrome architectural engraving of the original Penn Station waiting room

items.name: THE DODO
items.epitaph: It became the symbol of extinction after disappearing before extinction was understood.
items.why: Hunting, habitat disturbance, and introduced animals devastated a flightless bird adapted to life on Mauritius.
items.afterlife: A few remains, subfossil bones, historical descriptions, and modern reconstructions are all that survive.
items.note: The last reliable sighting is generally dated to 1662, although later possible dates remain debated.
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a dodo in Mauritius forest

items.name: INTERNET EXPLORER
items.epitaph: For years, the web arrived through a blue ‘e’—whether users chose it or not.
items.why: Modern browsers overtook it while Microsoft replaced it with Edge and retired the IE11 desktop application.
items.afterlife: IE mode and Trident compatibility remain available for organisations that still depend on legacy websites.
items.note: The 2022 date applies to the Internet Explorer 11 desktop application on certain Windows 10 versions; IE mode remains supported in Microsoft Edge.
items.image_alt: Monochrome engraving of a late-1990s computer displaying Internet Explorer

items.name: THE NEW YORK SUBWAY TOKEN
items.epitaph: For fifty years, one small brass coin opened the city beneath the streets.
items.why: MetroCard automation replaced tokens with stored-value and unlimited-ride magnetic cards.
items.afterlife: Collectors, jewellery, museum displays, and the token’s cut-out Y preserve a pocket-sized city symbol.
items.note: Tokens went off sale on 12 April 2003 and were accepted on the subway through 4 May 2003.
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a New York subway token beside a turnstile

items.name: THE PAPER AIRLINE TICKET
items.epitaph: The journey once began with a document too valuable to lose.
items.why: Electronic ticket records were cheaper, easier to update, and impossible for passengers to leave at home.
items.afterlife: Old ticket wallets, coupons, stubs, and collectors preserve the paperwork of commercial flight.
items.note: The date refers specifically to IATA ending paper ticket stock for its agency system on 1 June 2008, not every paper travel document.
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a paper airline ticket wallet, coupon, and luggage tag

items.name: SKYPE
items.epitaph: The call that made distance feel free finally went quiet.
items.why: Microsoft retired the consumer service to focus its free communication products on Teams.
items.afterlife: Its ringtone, usernames, chat histories, and role in normalising internet calls remain part of online culture.
items.note: Skype launched in 2003 and Microsoft retired the consumer service on 5 May 2025; Skype for Business is separate.
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum illustration of a desktop video call setup with webcam and headset

items.name: THE DOMESTIC ICEBOX
items.epitaph: Keeping food cold once meant waiting for a heavy block of winter.
items.why: Affordable electric refrigerators held steadier temperatures without daily ice deliveries, meltwater, or lost storage space.
items.afterlife: Antique cabinets, ice-delivery cards, tongs, and family stories preserve the household ritual of the iceman.
items.note: The endpoint is approximate: American households increasingly replaced iceboxes with affordable electric refrigerators during the 1930s.
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum illustration of a wooden domestic icebox with an ice block and delivery tools

items.name: MIR SPACE STATION
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of the completed Mir space station above Earth
items.epitaph: Fifteen years in orbit ended with a deliberate fall into the South Pacific.
items.why: Russia retired Mir as ageing systems and limited funding shifted attention toward the International Space Station.
items.afterlife: Museum hardware, photographs, research records, and the Shuttle–Mir programme preserve its orbital legacy.
items.note: Mir's first module launched in 1986; the station was deliberately deorbited on 23 March 2001.

items.name: NETSCAPE NAVIGATOR
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a 1990s computer displaying an early web browser
items.epitaph: The browser that opened the early web lost the browser war, then handed its code legacy onward.
items.why: AOL ended development after years of declining market share and directed remaining users toward Firefox.
items.afterlife: Mozilla and Firefox carried forward much of its open-source code lineage and browser culture.
items.note: AOL ended official Netscape browser support on 1 March 2008; existing copies continued to run.

items.name: AOL DIAL-UP INTERNET
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a 1990s computer, dial-up modem, telephone, and trial discs
items.epitaph: The handshake that announced the internet finally fell silent after thirty-four years.
items.why: Broadband, fibre, mobile networks, and satellite access made telephone-line internet obsolete.
items.afterlife: Modems, trial discs, connection tones, and the memory of tying up the phone line preserve its era.
items.note: AOL discontinued its dial-up internet service and associated dialer software on 30 September 2025.

items.name: THE HUIA
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of female and male Huia showing their different bills
items.epitaph: Its white-tipped feathers outlasted the forest voice that wore them.
items.why: Introduced mammal predators and hunting likely drove this New Zealand forest bird to extinction.
items.afterlife: Museum specimens and cultural memory preserve this distinctive bird.
items.note: 1907 is the last accepted sighting. Some huia likely survived into the 1920s; the exact extinction date is unknown.

items.name: RMS QUEEN MARY PASSENGER SERVICE
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of RMS Queen Mary at sea during her passenger-service years
items.epitaph: The Atlantic crossing became a destination only after the aeroplane made it unnecessary.
items.why: Cunard sold the ageing liner after 31 years on North Atlantic routes, ending her passenger voyages in 1967.
items.afterlife: Queen Mary remains permanently moored in Long Beach as a preserved ship, hotel, museum, and event venue.
items.note: The official timeline records the last eastbound transatlantic crossing as Voyage 513 in September 1967; the ship survives.

items.name: THE BRAMBLE CAY MELOMYS
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a Bramble Cay melomys on its low coral-cay habitat
items.epitaph: A small island mammal disappeared as the sea erased the ground beneath it.
items.why: Rising seas and extreme inundation destroyed most vegetation on its only known low-lying island habitat.
items.afterlife: Museum specimens and field records preserve a warning from a species lost within living memory.
items.note: Last seen in 2009 and declared extinct by Australia in 2019; possible occurrence in Papua New Guinea remains unproven.

items.name: THE SR.N4 CHANNEL HOVERCRAFT
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of an SR.N4 Mk III cross-Channel hovercraft at speed
items.epitaph: The ferry that flew above the Channel lost its race to tunnels and faster ships.
items.why: Ageing craft and high maintenance costs ended regular cross-Channel car-hovercraft service.
items.afterlife: Princess Anne survives at the Hovercraft Museum as the sole surviving Dover–Calais SR.N4.
items.note: The final Hoverspeed services ran over the weekend of 1 October 2000; the Hovercraft Museum preserves Princess Anne.

items.name: THE CARIBBEAN MONK SEAL
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a Caribbean monk seal resting on a sandy cay
items.epitaph: The Caribbean's only native seal vanished from waters that once held it by the thousands.
items.why: Centuries of intensive hunting for oil and food drove the species toward extinction.
items.afterlife: Museum specimens, historical accounts, and DNA studies preserve the lost seal's place among monk seals.
items.note: 1952 is the last confirmed sighting; NOAA declared the species extinct and removed it from the U.S. list in 2008.

items.name: LASERDISC PLAYERS
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a LaserDisc player, two large optical discs, and a CRT television
items.epitaph: The future once arrived on a silver platter the size of a record.
items.why: DVD and Blu-ray dominated home video while scarce parts made the last players difficult to manufacture.
items.afterlife: Collectors, film archives, arcade hardware, and preserved discs keep the analogue optical format spinning.
items.note: Pioneer announced on 14 January 2009 that it would end LaserDisc-player production after about 3,000 final units.

items.name: GOOGLE HANGOUTS
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a laptop, phone, and webcam in a group video call
items.epitaph: The chat window that gathered messages and video calls was redirected into another room.
items.why: Google migrated remaining users and most conversations to Google Chat as it consolidated communication products.
items.afterlife: Archived conversations, screenshots, and Google Takeout exports preserve its decade of chats and calls.
items.note: Google introduced the cross-platform Hangouts service in 2013 and made it unavailable in November 2022.

items.name: THE SEGWAY PT
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of an original Segway PT on an empty urban promenade
items.epitaph: The machine promised to reinvent walking, then rolled into tours, patrols, and punchlines.
items.why: The original self-balancing transporter remained a niche product as lighter electric mobility took over.
items.afterlife: Surviving machines, city tours, collectors, and later Segway-branded scooters preserve its unlikely silhouette.
items.note: Segway ended production of the original Personal Transporter on 15 July 2020; the wider Segway brand continued.

items.name: THE CHRISTMAS ISLAND PIPISTRELLE
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a Christmas Island pipistrelle in flight above rainforest
items.epitaph: The island's smallest bat faded until one final call crossed an unattended detector.
items.why: A rapid decline linked to introduced predators and ecological disruption ended before rescue could succeed.
items.afterlife: Museum specimens, acoustic records, and the failed rescue effort preserve an urgent conservation lesson.
items.note: Its last echolocation call was detected in August 2009; Australia formally listed the species as extinct in 2021.

items.name: THE PRINTED UK YELLOW PAGES
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum still life of an open telephone directory beside a corded landline
items.epitaph: The book that knew every local business was finally outnumbered by search boxes.
items.why: Online search and Yell's digital marketplace replaced the need to print and deliver regional directories.
items.afterlife: Final editions, phone-box memories, recycled paper, and Yell's online service preserve the yellow book.
items.note: Yell says the UK directory launched in 1966 and its final printed issue was distributed in 2019.

items.name: MICROSOFT KINECT
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum still life of a three-aperture motion sensor before a television
items.epitaph: It asked players to become the controller, then watched the living room move on.
items.why: Unbundling and limited game support left the motion sensor without a lasting console role.
items.afterlife: Researchers, artists, hackers, rehabilitation projects, and later depth cameras carried its ideas forward.
items.note: Microsoft executives confirmed on 25 October 2017 that manufacturing had ended after about 35 million units.

items.name: WOOLWORTHS UK
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum engraving of a closing British high-street variety store
items.epitaph: The red-fronted high-street variety store closed its last tills just short of a century.
items.why: Administration during the financial crisis ended the chain after falling sales and failed rescue efforts.
items.afterlife: Memories, shop signs, pick-and-mix counters, archives, and an unrelated online brand preserve its name.
items.note: The remaining 200 of Woolworths' 807 UK stores were scheduled to close on 6 January 2009.

items.name: THE XERCES BLUE BUTTERFLY
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a Xerces blue butterfly on deerweed
items.epitaph: San Francisco's iridescent blue vanished as its coastal dunes became a city.
items.why: Urban development destroyed and fragmented the specialised dune habitat on which the butterfly depended.
items.afterlife: Museum specimens, genomic research, habitat restoration, and silvery blue stand-ins carry its warning forward.
items.note: The Academy describes the Xerces blue as extinct and records its disappearance from San Francisco in 1943.

items.name: BOEING 747 PRODUCTION
items.image_alt: Monochrome technical engraving of an unbranded Boeing 747-8 freighter on a factory apron
items.epitaph: The jumbo jet that made the world smaller left the factory after 1,574 aircraft.
items.why: Efficient twin-engine widebodies displaced four-engine jets on most passenger and freight routes.
items.afterlife: Passenger and cargo fleets, Air Force One, museum aircraft, and surviving classics keep its silhouette aloft.
items.note: Boeing delivered the 1,574th and final 747 on 31 January 2023; existing aircraft remain in service.

items.name: ORKUT
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum still life of a mid-2000s computer displaying an early social-network profile
items.epitaph: The social network of scraps, testimonials, and communities signed off after ten years.
items.why: Google retired Orkut after the growth of YouTube, Blogger, and Google+ outpaced it.
items.afterlife: Exported profiles, screenshots, community memories, and its founder's revived homepage preserve its social web.
items.note: Google announced on 30 June 2014 that Orkut would shut down on 30 September 2014, ten years after launch.

items.name: MINIDISC PLAYERS
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum still life of portable and tabletop MiniDisc players, a disc cartridge, and earphones
items.epitaph: The pocket recorder that promised to replace tape was compressed by the MP3 age.
items.why: Flash-memory players and downloadable music made recordable optical discs less convenient.
items.afterlife: Used decks, blank discs, live recordings, and a devoted collector scene keep the format spinning.
items.note: Sony announced that its final batch of MiniDisc players would ship in March 2013 before manufacturing stopped.

items.name: THE FALKLAND ISLANDS WOLF
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history engraving of a Falkland Islands wolf in windswept tussac grass
items.epitaph: The islands' only native land mammal trusted people until they hunted it away.
items.why: Settlers poisoned and shot the tame canid for fur and to protect sheep.
items.afterlife: Museum skins, bones, Darwin's warning, and the Warrah's island names preserve its memory.
items.source_name: Falkland Islands Museum and National Trust
items.note: The museum says the last Warrah was said to have been killed at Shallow Bay in 1876; the asterisk preserves that historical uncertainty.

items.name: BETAMAX VIDEOCASSETTES
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum still life of a top-loading Betamax deck, compact videocassette, and CRT television
items.epitaph: The format that lost the videotape war kept recording long after the battle was over.
items.why: VHS offered longer recording time and wider industry support before digital media displaced tape entirely.
items.afterlife: Home recordings, surviving decks, broadcast relatives, archives, and collectors preserve the smaller cassette.
items.note: Sony introduced Betamax in 1975, ended recorder production in 2002, and ended cassette shipments in March 2016.

items.name: MERCURY AUTOMOBILES
items.image_alt: Monochrome automotive engraving of an unbadged 1967 Mercury Cougar on a dealership forecourt
items.epitaph: Ford's middle marque spent seventy-two years between Ford and Lincoln, then left the showroom.
items.why: Falling sales and overlap with Ford models led the company to concentrate on Ford and Lincoln.
items.afterlife: Surviving Cougars, Comets, Marauders, Grand Marquis cars, clubs, and archives preserve the marque.
items.note: Production ceased in late 2010 and the final Mercury, a Grand Marquis, left the line on 4 January 2011; the asterisk preserves the boundary.

items.name: SWISSAIR
items.image_alt: Monochrome museum portrait of a grounded four-engine Swiss passenger jet before an Alpine horizon
items.epitaph: The flying bank became the airline whose grounded fleet shocked a nation.
items.why: An expensive acquisition strategy, heavy losses, and a liquidity crisis brought the airline down.
items.afterlife: Aircraft, uniforms, posters, archives, and successor Swiss preserve the identity of the national carrier.
items.source_name: Swiss National Museum and Swiss Federal Archives
items.note: Swissair was founded in 1931 and grounded in October 2001; limited flights and the legal transition continued, so the endpoint is marked uncertain.

items.name: WINDOWS PHONE
items.image_alt: Monochrome product portrait of two smartphones displaying a grid of live tiles
items.epitaph: Its tiles were different and elegant—and surrounded by apps that never arrived.
items.why: Limited market share and a persistent shortage of major apps left Microsoft's mobile platform behind Android and iOS.
items.afterlife: Lumia hardware, Metro design, live tiles, and surviving devices preserve Microsoft's distinct phone interface.
items.note: Microsoft ended support for the final Windows 10 Mobile release on 10 December 2019; some services and one additional update continued briefly, so the endpoint is marked uncertain.

items.name: THE KEPLER SPACE TELESCOPE
items.epitaph: It ran out of fuel after proving that planets are more common than stars.
items.why: After nine years of planet hunting, the spacecraft exhausted the fuel needed for further science operations.
items.afterlife: Its public data, thousands of confirmed worlds, successor missions, and safe solar orbit extend its discoveries.
items.note: NASA retired Kepler on 30 October 2018 after it ran out of fuel; the mission had confirmed more than 2,600 exoplanets at retirement.
items.image_alt: Monochrome artistic illustration of Kepler with its photometer aperture and fixed solar array.

items.name: THE XBOX 360 STORE
items.epitaph: The shop closed. The games people already owned kept playing.
items.why: Microsoft retired purchases on the ageing console storefront as its platform moved to newer Xbox systems.
items.afterlife: Owned games, re-downloads, physical discs and backward-compatible purchases on newer systems continued.
items.note: New purchases ended on 29 July 2024, not console gameplay. Multiplayer remained publisher-dependent. Xbox Wire confirms the scope; GameSpot reported the closure day: https://www.gamespot.com/articles/the-xbox-360-store-shuts-down-for-good-today/1100-6525372/. The generic shop screen is symbolic artwork, not a historical UI screenshot.
items.image_alt: Interpretive monochrome illustration of a 2005 Xbox 360, wireless controller and symbolic storefront screen.
